items.title: Continual Adaptation for Pacific Indigenous Speech Recognition
items.authors: Yang Xiao(The University of Melbourne); Aso Mahmudi(The University of Melbourne); Nick Thieberger(The University of Melbourne); Eliathamby Ambikairajah(UNSW Sydney); Eun-Jung Holden(The University of Melbourne); Ting Dang(The University of Melbourne)
items.abstract: Speech foundation models struggle with low-resource Pacific Indigenous languages because of severe data scarcity. Furthermore, full fine-tuning risks catastrophic forgetting. To address this gap, we present an empirical study adapting models to real-world Pacific datasets. We investigate the impact of data volume, adaptation strategies, and representational drift on speech foundation models for various Pacific languages. Additionally, we analyze a continual learning framework for sequential language acquisition. Empirical results across three distinct Pacific Indigenous languages demonstrate that adapting to these linguistically distant languages induces severe internal representational drift. Consequently, these models face a strict plasticity and stability dilemma. While LoRA adapts well initially, it suffers from catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning. Ultimately, this study highlights the urgent need for robust adaptation strategies tailored to underrepresented languages.

items.title: Scaling Self-Supervised Speech Models Uncovers Deep Linguistic Relationships: Evidence from the Pacific Cluster
items.authors: Minu Kim(KAIST; University of Southern California); Hoirin Kim(KAIST); David R. Mortensen(Carnegie Mellon University)
items.abstract: Similarities between language representations derived from Self-Supervised Speech Models (S3Ms) have been observed to primarily reflect geographic proximity or surface typological similarities driven by recent expansion or contact, potentially missing deeper genealogical signals. We investigate how scaling an S3M-based language identification system from 126 to 4,017 languages reshapes this topology, and find a non-linear effect: phylogenetic recovery stays flat up to the 1K scale, but the 4K model undergoes a qualitative shift, resolving both clear lineages and long-term linguistic contact. Most strikingly, a robust Pacific macro-cluster emerges, grouping genealogically unrelated Papuan, Oceanic, and Australian languages--and we trace its driver to a concentrated encoding that captures shared acoustic signatures such as global energy dynamics. These results suggest that massive S3Ms internalize multiple layers of language history, offering a promising perspective for computational phylogenetics and the study of language contact.

items.title: Speech Recognition to Accelerate Documentation of Marquesan and Cook Islands Māori
items.authors: Marie Teikitohe(University of French Polynesia); Rolando Coto-Solano(Dartmouth College); Sally Akevai Nicholas(University of Auckland)
items.abstract: In this paper we report on the training of ASR for Marquesan. We collected 17 hours of transcribed naturalistic speech from L1 speakers and used this data to perform three experiments: (i) We used multilingual speech foundation models to finetune a monolingual Marquesan model. Wav2Vec2 had the best results, with a median CER=16 and WER=30. (ii) We used data from another Polynesian language, Cook Islands Maori, to train transfer and joint models. The joint model showed a minimal improvement for Marquesan (CER=15.4, WER=30.8), but there were no gains for CIM. (iii) We ran an experiment to determine if transcriptions produced by ASR actually represent a gain of time in the language documentation process. When human transcribers corrected from an ASR transcription, this work was between 0.7x and 2.4x faster than when the audio was transcribed completely manually. We expect to integrate ASR into the documentation workflow to make the materials available to the Marquesan-speaking community.

items.title: Mapping Acceptable Pronunciation Range for te reo Māori through Perceptual, Acoustic, and Marker Evaluative Data
items.authors: Zoe E Evans(University of Auckland); Catherine I Watson(University of Auckland); Peter J Keegan(University of Auckland); Jesin James(University of Auckland); Piata Allen(University of Auckland)
items.abstract: Pronunciation teaching assumes a canonical target. Yet speech varies across speakers and generations, meaning targets are better understood as ranges of acceptable pronunciation. For many languages, including ones subject to major revitalisation efforts like New Zealand's te reo Māori, these ranges are not documented. We developed a method triangulating acoustic measures, phonetician transcription, and fluent speaker evaluation to map acceptable variation in Māori vowels. Examining the monophthongs /a u/ and diphthongs /ai ae au/, we found a clear asymmetry: variants acceptable as monophthongs were penalised in diphthongs. This challenges the widespread view of diphthongs as vowel sequences - if they were simply concatenations, acceptability would transfer across contexts. Our findings suggest fluent speakers treat diphthongs as unit phonemes with distinct acceptability boundaries, implying they should be taught as distinct sounds rather than extension of monophthong instruction.

items.title: Oral stop realisation in three French Polynesian languages
items.authors: Janet Fletcher(University of Melbourne); Adele Gregory(University of Melbourne)
items.abstract: Seven distinct indigenous languages are spoken in French Polynesia in the Eastern Pacific region. This study explores voice onset time (VOT) and voiceless stop realisation in three languages: Tahitian, Marquesan (Northern and Southern), and Rurutu. All languages are considered to have relatively low levels of inter-generational transmission. The results show stops in all three languages are voiceless and short lag with mean VOT values of around 20 ms. Reflecting a well-observed crosslinguistic pattern, velars in Marquesan have longer VOT than bilabials and dentals in either of the three languages. Following vowel has the strongest influence on VOT duration with longer values for /t/ preceding close front vowels, and for /p/ preceding close back rounded vowels across the corpus. Closure duration is influenced by prosodic factors in Tahitian only, with longer durations in accented versus unaccented stops. Voicing proportion levels are low with slightly longer values in medial contexts but overall, there is no strong evidence of voicing or manner lenition in the current corpus.

items.title: A preliminary exploration of stop-vowel coarticulation in Māori
items.authors: Isabella Shields(University of Auckland); Hiraia Haami-Wells(University of Auckland); C. T. Justine Hui(University of Auckland); Peter J. Keegan(University of Auckland); Catherine I. Watson(University of Auckland)
items.abstract: Te reo Māori (the Māori language) is the indigenous language of New Zealand. Māori phonetics research has predominantly focused on vowels and diphthongs, however there has been limited exploration of coarticulatory processes which may influence vowel realisation. This study presents a preliminary investigation of the coarticulatory impacts of oral stop consonants on vowels in M¯aori, drawing on a new read-speech corpus of 7 fluent female speakers of Māori. A total of 524 stressed vowel tokens, occurring across different stop contexts (/p t k/), are analysed. Using Generalised Additive Mixed Models (GAMMs) to analyse first and second formants, it is shown that consonant context significantly influences these measures, suggesting consonant coarticulation results in notable changes to vowel quality, particularly backness. The implications of these findings are discussed with respect to our understanding of vowel and consonant variation in Māori.

items.title: Vavanagi: a Community-run Platform for Documentation of the Hula Language in Papua New Guinea
items.authors: Bri Olewale(Vula'a Kunenai Community); Raphael Merx(University of Melbourne); Ekaterina Vylomova(University of Melbourne)
items.abstract: We present Vavanagi, a community-run platform for Hula (Vula'a), an Austronesian language of Papua New Guinea with approximately 10,000 speakers. Vavanagi supports crowd sourced English-Hula text translation and voice recording, with elder-led review and community-governed data infrastructure. To date, 77 translators and 4 reviewers have produced over 12k parallel sentence pairs covering 9k unique Hula words. We also propose multi-level framework for measuring community involvement, from consultation to fully community-initiated and governed projects. We position Vavanagi at Level 5: initiative, design, implementation, and data governance all sit within the Hula community, making it, to our knowledge, the first community-led language technology initiative for a language of this size. Vavanagi shows how language technology can bridge village-based and urban members, connect generations, and support cultural heritage on the community's own terms.

items.title: Working Together on Technologies: A Case Study of Collaboration in Aotearoa
items.authors: Ben Hutchinson(Google Australia); Gabriella Conlon(Independent); Greg Duncum(Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori); Carrie Jones(Google New Zealand); Tāne Karamaina(Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori); Hautahi Kingi(Google USA); Jamie Towler(Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori); Caroline Rainsford(Google New Zealand); Ngahiwi Apanui-Barr(Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori)
items.abstract: Te reo Māori (the Māori language) has historically been poorly served by technologies which English and other global languages take for granted. One such class of technologies is Text-to-Speech (TTS), which is used into a wide array of technology products. These range from screen readers which support accessibility, through to products which support hands- and eyes-free use while driving, such as reading aloud driving direction guidance. This paper presents a case study of collaboration on TTS technologies between Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori and Google. The former is a Māori-led organisation, the latter a global technology company. This case study focuses not on technical implementation details, but rather on the challenges in the partnership to mutual understanding and alignment, and the processes we co-developed to overcome those challenges, which led to the successful development of technology which was satisfactory to both partners.

items.title: Pā‑Kakare: The First Emotional Speech Database for Te Reo Māori
items.authors: Himashi Rathnayake(University of Auckland); Jesin James(University of Auckland); Ake Nicholas(University of Auckland); Gianna Leoni(Te Hiku Media); Catherine I. Watson(University of Auckland); Peter J. Keegan(University of Auckland)
items.abstract: This paper introduces Pā-Kakare, the first emotional speech database for te reo Māori, the Indigenous language of New Zealand. Unlike existing emotional speech resources that rely on presumed universal emotions, this corpus uses 16 categories identified through prior community-based research, ensuring cultural relevance. The database contains 3,840 high-quality recordings from four professional Māori actors, with 15 sentences per emotion, designed to capture both neutral-context and emotion-salient content. We describe emotion selection, corpus design, recording procedures, and database validation. A preliminary acoustic analysis shows systematic differences in fundamental frequency, intensity, and speech rate across the emotion categories. As one of the first emotional speech corpora for an Indigenous Pacific language, Pā-Kakare supports the analysis of Māori emotional expression and encourages further research on emotional speech in under-represented languages.

items.title: Automating Sociophonetic Research in Under-Resourced Languages: A Case Study of Speech Rate in Cook Islands Māori
items.authors: Rolando Coto-Solano(Dartmouth College); Sally Akevai Nicholas(University of Auckland)
items.abstract: In this paper we test the use of artificial intelligence tools, such as speech recognition and age detection, to gather a large corpus and semi-automate the description of sociophonetic phenomena. Our case study was speech rate variation across different islands and age groups in the Cook Islands, a previously unreported phenomenon for this language. We gathered a corpus that combined fieldwork and online data and used speech recognition to calculate speech rate (moras/second) for 60 speakers of Cook Islands Māori, recorded in a total of 7.5 hours of audio. Automatically calculating age from speakers' faces did not yield good results and had to be done manually. As for the sociophonetics, in some islands, like the Nga Pū Toru group, younger speakers have a significantly faster speech rate. However, islands like Rarotonga and Aitutaki do not show this pattern, which might be due to language shift in the younger generation. Future research will include more islands and speakers.

items.title: The Sound of Code-Switching: Prosodic Profiles of Spontaneous Spanish-English Speech
items.authors: Debasmita Bhattacharya(Columbia University); Michela Marchini(University of Michigan); Julia Hirschberg(Columbia University)
items.abstract: Code-switching (CSW) has been studied via many linguistic frameworks, but little is known about the prosody of such multilingual speech. We ask: Is CSW prosodically different from monolingual productions in spontaneous conversation, and how are variations influenced by speaker proficiency and the multilingual properties of such speech? To answer these, we examine a large-scale Spanish-English corpus over a host of language-independent prosodic features, finding that CSW prosody differs meaningfully from monolingual prosody in both English and Spanish, with greater influence on this variation coming from speaker-specific factors. Our work is the first to apply such a language-generalizable, macro-level, and model-diagnostic approach to studying spontaneous CSW prosody, and provides novel insights into multilinguality that have potential implications for the synthesis of naturalistic code-switched speech.

items.title: Gradient phonetic detail is less detrimental to word segmentation in infant-directed speech
items.authors: Gabriel Scharff(University of California Los Angeles); Megha Sundara(University of California Los Angeles)
items.abstract: Computational models of word segmentation typically represent speech as sequences of phonemes, as in a dictionary, but real speech contains substantial phonetic variation. In previous research on adult-directed speech, encoding phonetic variation has been found to degrade the ability of many algorithms to detect word boundaries. We tested whether encoding phonetic detail also degrades detection of word boundaries by word segmentation algorithms when tested on infant-directed speech. Infant- and adult-directed speech differ in many ways: infant-directed speech contains shorter words, more isolated single word utterances, and a smaller vocabulary. Two of the four algorithms evaluated showed no degradation in word segmentation performance, with the other two showing only modest degradation compared to previous reports on adult-directed speech. These results suggest that finding words in infant-directed speech may be more robust to phonetic variation in the input than previously assumed.

items.title: Word Iconicity and Phonological Surprisal as Predictors of Age of Acquisition
items.authors: Alexander Kilpatrick(University of Aizu); Rikke Bundgaard-Nielsen(University of Melbourne)
items.abstract: Iconic words are acquired earlier than arbitrary words cross-linguistically and controlled experiments show that children find phonotactically typical word forms easier to learn than unusual ones. This contrasts with adult processing, where unusual word forms-including iconic words-are better recalled and more deeply encoded. Using machine learning and regression analyses, we examine the relationship between iconicity, information-theoretic measures of phonological surprisal and entropy, and age of acquisition (AoA). Iconicity robustly predicts earlier AoA across the lexicon, while surprisal and entropy show weak and inconsistent effects on acquisition but substantially predict adult processing outcomes. These findings reveal a developmental dissociation: form-meaning transparency scaffolds early word learning, while phonological unpredictability supports adult processing efficiency.

items.title: Non-linear Effects of Semantic Relevance on Word Duration in Spontaneous Speech
items.authors: Kun Sun(Tongji University); Rong Wang(University of Tübingen)
items.abstract: Word duration in spontaneous speech reflects interactions between lexical access, contextual predictability, and speech planning. While effects of word length, lexical frequency, and speaking rate are well established, semantic context is typically approximated indirectly and modeled linearly. In this study, we investigate whether semantic relevance, a metric that quantifies the semantic relatedness between a target word and its local context, predicts word duration in conversational speech. Using the Buckeye Corpus, we analyze word-level timing data with generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) to capture potential non-linear effects while accounting for speaker variability and established linguistic controls. Results show that semantic relevance is a significant predictor of word duration, independent of word frequency and length. Exploratory analyses suggest that its effect may be frequency-dependent. Increased semantic relevance generally facilitates production, but highly context-central words exhibit longer durations, particularly for low-frequency items. These findings demonstrate that semantic relevance captures production-specific contextual effects on speech timing beyond linear approximations and highlight fundamental differences between language production and comprehension.

items.title: From Words to Sentences: Contextual Predictability Overrides Phonetic Ambiguity in Lexical Competition
items.authors: Will Chih-Chao Chang(University of California); Jiaxuan Li(University of California); Xin Xie(University of California)
items.abstract: Prior work shows that for isolated word recognition, sub-phonemic variation modulates lexical competition in a graded manner. Whether this modulation persists when sentence context is available, however, remains unknown. We conducted two cross-modal priming experiments using acoustically manipulated English minimal pairs. Experiment 1 (isolated words) replicated the gradient effect of phonetic ambiguity, driven by differences in sub-phonemic variation, on lexical competition. In Experiment 2 (sentences), however, while lexical competition was better resolved in high- than low-predictability contexts, this competition was no longer modulated by phonetic ambiguity. Our findings support theoretical accounts such as predictive coding and Bayesian inference models, where top-down expectations reduce the contribution of bottom-up signals to lexical competition. These results suggest that models of spoken word recognition built on isolated words may not fully extend to sentence comprehension.

items.title: Informativity of high-frequency bands on the place of articulation shift in retroflex sibilants produced by children
items.authors: Oliwia Skórzewska(Silesian University of Technology); Maria Filipek(Silesian University of Technology); Wojciech Pieniazek(Silesian University of Technology); Zuzanna Miodońska(Silesian University of Technology)
items.abstract: Sibilant fricatives are characterized by their spectral frication noise, which is sensitive to articulatory variations. Sibilants prone to articulatory distortions, making them key targets for early assessment in speech diagnosis. Those non-normative sibilant productions are collectively referred to as sigmatism. We analyzed retroflex fricative and affricate productions from 186 Polish preschool children. Analyses focused on four places of articulation: retroflex (normative), dental, postalveolar, and interdental. We extracted 34 frame-level features characterizing frication noise of Polish sibilants, including noise energies, integrated energy over fricative formants, and their ratios. Linear mixed-effects models were used to robustly quantify articulatory variation. High-frequency energy up to 16 kHz carried diagnostically relevant information for pediatric speech distortions, and newly introduced features provided a voicing-independent measure across different retroflex sibilants.

items.title: Learning Emotion-discriminative Representations for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Speech Emotion Recognition
items.authors: Jinyi Mi(Nagoya University); Ding Ma(Nagoya University); Tomoki Toda(Nagoya University)
items.abstract: Zero-shot cross-lingual speech emotion recognition (SER) remains challenging due to distribution mismatches across languages and the lack of emotion annotations in target language. Under such conditions, models trained solely on source-language data frequently suffer from degraded generalization when evaluated on unseen target languages. To address this limitation, we propose an emotion-discriminative representation learning method that integrates supervised contrastive learning and speaker adversarial learning. The contrastive learning promotes cross-lingual emotion alignment, while speaker adversarial learning suppresses speaker-related cues to encourage speaker-invariant representations. Experimental results under a zero-shot cross-lingual SER setting demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves SER performance over conventional training strategies.

items.title: Quantifying Cross-Lingual Transfer in Paralinguistic Speech Tasks
items.authors: Pol Buitrago(BSC; UPC); Oriol Pareras(BSC); Federico Costa(Barcelona Supercomputing Center; Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya); Javier Hernando(Barcelona Supercomputing Center; Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya)
items.abstract: Paralinguistic speech tasks are often considered relatively language-agnostic, as they rely on extralinguistic acoustic cues rather than lexical content. However, prior studies report performance degradation under cross-lingual conditions, indicating non-negligible language dependence. Still, these studies typically focus on isolated language pairs or task-specific settings, limiting comparability and preventing a systematic assessment of task-level language dependence. We introduce the Cross-Lingual Transfer Matrix (CLTM), a systematic method to quantify cross-lingual interactions between pairs of languages within a given task. We apply the CLTM to two paralinguistic tasks, gender identification and speaker verification, using a multilingual HuBERT-based encoder, to analyze how donor-language data affects target-language performance during fine-tuning. Our results reveal distinct transfer patterns across tasks and languages, reflecting systematic, language-dependent effects.

items.title: Synthetic Speech, Real Signal: Paralinguistic Preservation and Cross-Lingual Augmentation via Voice Cloning
items.authors: Roseline Polle(thymia); Owen Parsons(thymia); George Fairs(thymia); Luis Miguel San Martin Fernandez(thymia); Cole Looney(The University of Edinburgh); Xiaoliang Wu(University of Southampton); Alexandra Livia Georgescu(thymia); Stefano Goria(thymia)
items.abstract: Synthetic data augmentation in speech is common practice for linguistic tasks like ASR, but has seen far less work for paralinguistic ones, especially clinical tasks where labelled data is expensive and some patient groups are underrepresented. Voice cloning is one such augmentation approach, but is typically evaluated on speech intelligibility (WER) or speaker similarity (SS) rather than on downstream performance, and it remains unclear whether these preserve the paralinguistic signal such tasks depend on. We benchmark eight voice cloning models on five paralinguistic tasks across public and clinical datasets, showing most preserve signal with modest degradation. We then clone English clinical speech into Japanese and find that training on cloned data outperforms raw cross-lingual transfer for depression and anxiety detection on real Japanese speech, suggesting voice cloning is a promising direction for augmenting clinical speech data in low-resource languages.

items.title: Universality of Speech Emotion Recognition in Humans and Speech Language Models
items.authors: Yuka Tatsumi(Stanford University); Nathan Roll(Stanford University); Robert D. Hawkins(Stanford University); Meghan Sumner(Stanford University); Dan Jurafsky(Stanford University)
items.abstract: Humans can recognize the emotional content of speech in unfamiliar languages fairly accurately, a phenomenon known as universality. However, it remains unclear whether computational speech encoder models also exhibit universality in detecting emotions. This study compares 101 English monolingual human listeners and two English monolingual speech language models (SLMs) on cross-language recognition of basic emotions in French, Japanese, Greek, and Thai. Both humans and SLMs performed well above chance level, supporting universality. Yet we found differences across emotions: humans were more accurate for negative emotions and tended to default to neutral responses, whereas models performed best on and defaulted to happy and surprise. These findings demonstrate universality in SLM emotion recognition while highlighting that machines have distinct recognition patterns from humans, underscoring the need for cross-disciplinary study of emotion.

items.title: Human-like cross-language generalisation in deep neural speaker embeddings and its acoustic foundations
items.authors: Tianze Xu(University of Zurich); Xiyang Li(University of Zurich); Xiaoming Jiang(Shanghai International Studies University); Volker Dellwo(University of Zurich)
items.abstract: Generalisability is a central question for deep neural networks, including the cross-language generalisation of speaker embeddings. This study examined whether deep neural speaker embeddings generalise across languages and how such generalisation relates to human perception and acoustic structure. Using Cantonese–English bilingual speech presented in within- and cross-language conditions, we derived similarity from 18 state-of-the-art models and compared it with human ratings and acoustic features using linear mixed models and representational similarity analysis. Embeddings exhibited cross-language generalisation that broadly paralleled human behaviour, reflecting accurate identity discrimination and sensitivity to language switching. This generalisation relied on largely shared acoustic cues with language-sensitive weighting, mirroring human patterns. Together, these findings provide converging evidence for human–machine alignment in cross-language voice similarity processing.

items.title: Speaker or Language? Explaining Variance in Charismatic Prosody Across Luxembourgish and French
items.authors: Nina Hosseini-Kivanani(University of Luxembourg; Radio Télévision Luxembourg); Nafiseh Taghva(Shiraz University); Peter Gilles(University of Luxembourg); Oliver Niebuhr(University of Southern Denmark)
items.abstract: Charismatic speech is shaped by language and speaking style, yet their relative contribution in bilingual public speaking remains unclear. We analyzed spontaneous speeches of 10 politicians who address audiences in Luxembourgish and French, in highly comparable communicative contexts across languages. From 400 utterances, we extracted 41 acoustic-prosodic features linked to vocal charisma and fitted mixed-effects models to separate speaker-vand language-related variance. Speaker identity accounted for most variance, whereas language explained less, but still showed systematic differences: French productions showed higher shimmer and phrase-final F0, indicative of a polite, respectful voice, while Luxembourgish productions exhibited stronger mid-frequency spectral energy, suggesting a more vocally present profile. These patterns align with the sociolinguistic roles of Luxembourgish as an informal identity language and French as a high-prestige institutional variety.

items.title: Improving Adversarial Robustness in Spoken Language Identification through Self-Defensive Distillation
items.authors: Spandan Dey(Samsung R&D Institute India-Bangalore)
items.abstract: Robustness against adversarial attacks is majorly explored for security-critical speech applications, such as speaker verification and speech recognition. Concerning their on-growing multilingual expansion, we present one of the first extensive studies on developing adversarial robustness for spoken language identification (LID). We show the vulnerability of state-of-the-art LID models under widely-explored white-box gradient-based adversarial attacks. We then propose a novel adversarial robust LID framework, Self-Defensive Adversarial Re-Training (SDART). It expands the conventional adversarial re-training with adversarial sample mining, teacher-free defensive distillation using dynamic online label smoothing, and linguistic consistency regularization. Across multiple databases and architectures, SDART outperforms several conventional adversarial robustness methods, improving performance on both genuine and adversarially attacked samples.

items.title: Probing the Layer-wise Geometry of Chinese Dialect Representations in Wav2Vec 2.0
items.authors: Zhen Peng(University of Science and Technology of China); Jiahong Yuan(University of Science and Technology of China)
items.abstract: While Wav2Vec 2.0 has achieved significant success in speech representation tasks, the mechanisms by which it encodes dialectal features across different layers remain underexplored. This study applies geometric probing methods to analyze the changes in the representations of five Chinese dialects within the model. Experimental results reveal a three-stage trajectory: (1) lower layers are dominated by fundamental acoustic discrepancies; (2) middle layers exhibit high spatial dispersion, preserving fine-grained phonetic details; and (3) deep layers show significant spatial contraction, though the resulting clustering remains consistent with traditional linguistic taxonomies. Based on these findings, this study suggests that for tasks requiring fine-grained phonetic information, such as accent identification, intermediate-layer features should be prioritized; and deep-layer features are more valuable for broad dialectal classification or phylogenetic analysis.

items.title: Robust Language Identification Using Semi-positive Contrastive Learning
items.authors: Shubham Sharma(Indian Institute of Technology Mandi); Padmanabhan Rajan(Indian Institute of Technology Mandi)
items.abstract: Conventionally, Spoken Language Identification is modeled as a speech-based language identification task, ignoring the importance of text data. This work addresses the cross-corpora generalization issue for the low-resourced spoken language identification (LID) problem. We propose Semi-positive Contrastive Learning (SpCL), a robust framework for LID that addresses domain shifts without requiring explicit domain adaptation or generalization. Our method uses a bi-modal audio-text encoder to map speech waveforms and phoneme-based text captions into a shared embedding space. By introducing a novel semi-positive contrastive loss, SpCL distinguishes strong positive pairs (same language and domain) from semi-positive pairs (same language, different domains) using a controlled weighting scheme. We experimented on 12 Indian languages using multi-domain datasets that demonstrate that SpCL outperforms strong acoustic and phonetic baselines, achieving superior accuracy on both seen and unseen test domains. Furthermore, we conducted ablation studies that confirm the benefits of semipositive weighting and dynamic captions, with Whisper-based audio encoders delivering the best robustness under domain mismatch.

items.title: Predict-Then-Adapt: Inferring Coordinates from Speech for Continuous Geo-Conditioned Dialectal ASR
items.authors: Pouya Mehralian(KU Leuven); Hugo Van hamme(KU Leuven)
items.abstract: Geo-conditioned adaptation can improve dialectal ASR, but most methods assume speaker coordinates are available at inference. We remove this dependency by inferring location from speech at test time and conditioning on the predicted coordinates. We attach a lightweight Coordinate Regression Head (CRH) to a frozen encoder and train it to regress latitude/longitude from utterance-level representations. Inference uses two passes: (i) predict coordinates with geo-conditioning disabled, then (ii) decode with geo-conditioning enabled conditioned on the prediction. CRH adds < 0.1% parameters and increases inference latency by < 3%. On Dutch dialects, CRH achieves 15-25 km mean great-circle error using 10-30 s of speech, and the GLoRIA method is robust to errors in this range. As a result, CRH+GLoRIA outperforms rank-matched LoRA and approaches oracle-coordinate adaptation performance, while preserving GLoRIA interpretability via analyzable coordinate-gated low-rank components.

items.title: Dialect Bias in Speech Recognition Across 10 Spanish and French Varieties
items.authors: Rodrigo Nieto(Stanford University; Google); Maria Angelika-Nikita(Stanford University); Diane Sarkis(Stanford University); Diyi Yang(Stanford University)
items.abstract: ASR bias research is largely English-focused and the mechanisms underlying performance disparities remain poorly understood. We address both gaps for Spanish and French. Using a 20-hour, gender-balanced corpus (the first for these languages designed for dialect bias analysis, with country-level stratification and manual transcripts preserving dialectal features), we benchmark seven models and find non-uniform disparities: models favor European varieties in French, while Spanish reveals unexpected patterns with Dominican outperforming Peninsular and with Chilean showing the highest error rates. Lexical analysis links failures to morphosyntactic "correction" and regional discourse markers; acoustic analysis shows that speaker embeddings encode dialect information; a diagnostic fine-tuning experiment localizes these errors to the decoder. Together, these results demonstrate that ASR errors systematically reflect linguistic distance from training distributions.

items.title: DASR-CPO: Reference-Free Contrastive Preference Optimization for Correcting Mandarin Semantic Drift in Low-Resource Chinese Dialect ASR
items.authors: Tao Zhang(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); haiyang Zhang(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications)
items.abstract: Pretrained ASR models such as Whisper-Large-v3 can degrade on low-resource Chinese dialects because a Mandarin-dominant prior favors frequent homophones. This causes Mandarin semantic drift: dialect words are transcribed as phonetically similar but semantically wrong Mandarin forms, often on entity- or keyword-critical spans. LoRA supervised fine-tuning reduces character error rate (CER) but does not explicitly suppress these competitors. We propose DASR-CPO, a reference-free contrastive preference optimization method that teaches the model to prefer dialect-correct spans over mined Mandarin confusions. Preference pairs come from data-driven confusion mining without manual annotation. We localize drift-prone spans by sequence matching and train with a span-level contrastive objective using hard negatives. On MagicData Sichuanese (4.53 h), DASR-CPO reduces CER from 24.85% to 22.58% and improves dialect-entity F1 from 72.82 to 74.15 with zero inference-time overhead.

items.title: Visually-Guided Spatial Audio Generation for 360° In-the-Wild Speech Scenes
items.authors: Qingyu Luo(University of Surrey); Peng Zhang(University of Surrey); Wenwu Wang(University of Surrey); Philip J.B. Jackson(University of Surrey)
items.abstract: Spatial audio is a key component of immersive 360° media, yet high-quality spatial capture remains limited in real-world speech-dominant scenes. We study visually guided First-Order Ambisonics (FOA) speech spatialization in the wild: given aligned 360° video and an omnidirectional audio track, we recover the missing directional FOA components. To support this task, we introduce YT-SPEECH, a speech-oriented 360° video-FOA dataset curated from YouTube. We propose a two-stage Localizer-Renderer framework, where an audio-visual segmentation backbone provides frame-wise spatial heatmaps and a conditional complex-domain U-Net reconstructs directional FOA signals from the omnidirectional channel. A confidence-based gating strategy stabilizes conditioning under ambiguous acoustic conditions. Experiments show improved reconstruction fidelity, spatial accuracy, and perceptual speech quality relative to ablated variants and prior approaches.

items.title: Room Impulse Response Completion Using Signal-Prediction Diffusion Models Conditioned on Simulated Early Reflections
items.authors: Zeyu Xu(International Audio Laboratories Erlangen); Andreas Brendel(IIS); Albert G. Prinn(International Audio Laboratories Erlangen); Emanuël A.P. Habets(International Audio Laboratories Erlangen)
items.abstract: Room impulse responses (RIRs) are fundamental to audio data augmentation, acoustic signal processing, and immersive audio rendering. While geometric simulators such as the image source method (ISM) can efficiently generate early reflections, they lack the realism of measured RIRs due to missing acoustic wave effects. We propose a diffusion-based RIR completion method using signal-prediction conditioned on ISM-simulated direct-path and early reflections. Unlike state-of-the-art methods, our approach imposes no fixed duration constraint on the input early reflections. We further incorporate classifier-free guidance to steer generation toward a target distribution learned from physically realistic RIRs simulated with the Treble SDK. Objective evaluation demonstrates that the proposed method outperforms a state-of-the-art baseline in early RIR completion and energy decay curve reconstruction.

items.title: U2A-Net: Physically Motivated Ultrasound‑to‑Audio Neural Modeling for Parametric Array Loudspeakers
items.authors: Mengtong Li(Nanjing University); Yu Sun(Samsung Electronics (China)); Jia-Xin Zhong(Nanjing University); Jing Lu(Nanjing University; Horizon Robotics)
items.abstract: Parametric array loudspeakers (PALs) provide directional sound for private speech applications but exhibit strong nonlinear behavior, making accurate modeling challenging. Recent deep learning methods typically adopt an audio-to-audio (A2A) framework that maps baseband audio input directly to audible outputs, which implicitly compounds ultrasonic modulation with airborne self-demodulation, demanding high complexity to resolve the integrated nonlinearity. Motivated by underlying physics, we propose U2A-Net, a multi-rate neural ultrasound-to-audio (U2A) framework that maps modulated ultrasonic signals to audible outputs. By decoupling the modulation process, U2A-Net focuses entirely on the intrinsic nonlinear self-demodulation. Experiments on a representative PAL show that U2A-Net consistently outperforms A2A networks and Volterra filters, achieving average nonlinear distortion modeling error below 1.62%, which highlight the advantage of physics-motivated reformulation for PAL modeling.

items.title: Echoes after Edits: Room Impulse Response Estimation for Geometry Update
items.authors: Swapnil Bhosale(MERL; University of Surrey); Yoshiki Masuyama(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL)); Moitreya Chatterjee(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL)); Christoph Boeddeker(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL)); Julius Richter(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL)); Gordon Wichern(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL)); Jonathan Le Roux(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL))
items.abstract: Room impulse responses (RIRs) characterize sound propagation in a scene, determined by its geometry and materials. Traditional RIR estimation relies on acoustic simulation, while recent deep learning focuses on spatial interpolation. However, acoustic simulation requires material annotation of each object, and interpolation requires multiple RIRs whenever the scene is edited slightly (e.g., rearranging furniture). Both approaches are inefficient and impractical in everyday environments. In this paper, we introduce edit-conditioned RIR estimation, which updates a measured RIR to reflect geometry edits. To relate the geometry edits to acoustic variation without material annotations, we simulate proxy RIRs from the room meshes before and after the edit using predefined materials. We propose PG-RIR, which leverages these proxies to estimate the variation in the real RIR. Experiments show that PG-RIR accurately predicts RIRs under furniture rearrangement and removal.

items.title: Dual-Geometry Manifolds for Few-shot RIR Prediction
items.authors: Swapnil Bhosale(MERL; University of Surrey); Gordon Wichern(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL)); Yoshiki Masuyama(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL)); Moitreya Chatterjee(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL)); Christoph Boeddeker(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL)); Julius Richter(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL)); Xiatian Zhu(University of Surrey); Jonathan Le Roux(Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories (MERL))
items.abstract: Few-shot room impulse response (RIR) prediction estimates target acoustics from sparse reference RIRs. Current models fuse references in a static Euclidean space, assuming a zero-curvature latent geometry for all temporal phases of the RIR. Using Gromov δ-hyperbolicity, we show the acoustic manifold's geometry evolves from a hierarchical tree structure during early reflections to a flat, diffuse late reverberation tail. Motivated by this heterogeneity, we propose Janus-RIR, a temporally gated, dual-geometry aggregation model. It employs a hyperbolic branch for early reflections and a Euclidean branch for smooth statistical averaging of the late tail, governed by a context-aware dynamic gate. Experiments on AcousticRooms show Janus-RIR achieves state-of-the-art. Aligning latent geometry with the physics of acoustics improves speech clarity (C50) while reducing late reverberation (T60) error by 26% over Euclidean baselines, adapting to environment-specific mixing times.

title: Low-Resource Speech Synthesis
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 7 - Oral 1 - Low-Resource Speech Synthesis

items.title: Low-Resource Speech Synthesis: What Have We Solved, and What Remains?
items.abstract: Speech synthesis has traditionally required substantial amounts of transcribed speech, limiting its availability to only a fraction of the world’s languages. Multilingual and cross-lingual transfer, learning from unpaired data, unsupervised speech-unit discovery, and more recently foundation models have dramatically reduced these requirements. Today, models can synthesize hundreds or even thousands of languages, sometimes with little or no transcribed speech in the target language. This talk surveys the key advances behind this progress and highlights what has been successfully addressed in low-resource speech synthesis. It then examines what remains challenging, particularly for genuinely under-resourced languages, including linguistic diversity, synthesis quality, and reliable evaluation. Finally, drawing on experiences from Indigenous and endangered language technology, I discuss how future progress can better connect advances in speech synthesis with the needs and priorities of language communities.

items.title: Lightweight Cross-Lingual Speaker Adaptation for Indic TTS
items.authors: Tarun Kumar(Indian Institue of Technology); Keshav Agarwal(Indian Institue of Technology); Pawan Goyal(Indian Institue of Technology); Laxmidhar Behera(Indian Institue of Technology); Hema A. Murthy(Indian Institue of Technology)
items.abstract: Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems have improved significantly, but most work focuses on high-resource languages, leaving Indian languages less explored. Voice-cloning models trained on Indic data often suffer from word-dropping errors and slow inference, making deployment difficult. We propose a lightweight speaker adaptation pipeline that uses only a 10-second reference sample. Synthetic speech generated from a voice-cloning model is filtered through a four-stage quality-control pipeline and used to fine-tune a FastSpeech2 model with dual-site speaker conditioning and a cosine consistency loss. Phoneme unification through the Common Label Set (CLS) enables the adapted voice to synthesize speech across Hindi, Marathi, Tamil, and Telugu without additional recordings. The resulting system produces deterministic outputs, runs 53x faster than the baseline, and improves intelligibility and naturalness while preserving speaker characteristics in cross-lingual synthesis.

items.title: Scalable Neural TTS for Latin-Script Low-Resource Languages of Manipur
items.authors: Hoomexsun Pangsatabam(National Institute of Technology Manipur); Khumanthem Chanchanbi(National Institute of Technology Manipur); Kansham Tungran Maring(National Institute of Technology Manipur); Yambem Jina Chanu(National Institute of Technology Manipur)
items.abstract: Many low-resource languages in Northeast India lack native scripts, limiting speech technology development. This work presents text-to-speech resources for two Manipuri tribal languages, Tangkhul (9.58h) and Maring(10.79h), based on studio recordings in their standard dialects. The dataset consists of read speech collected from textbooks, storybooks, and Bible translations, together with an automatic preprocessing pipeline for segmentation and normalization. We train monolingual character-level TTS systems using Tacotron 2 and FastSpeech 2 and evaluate them with objective and subjective metrics. The results show that these corpora and baseline systems can support TTS development for low-resource Latin-script languages of Manipur and provide a useful starting point for future work.

items.title: High-Quality Speech Synthesis for Under-Resourced Ethiopian Languages
items.authors: Rahel Mekonen Tamiru(Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute); Solomon Teferra Abate(Addis Ababa Unversty); Martha Yifiru Tachbelie(Addis Ababa Unversty); Abel Mulat Alemu(Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute); Samuel Rahimeto Kebede(Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute); Rosa Tsegaye Aga(Ethiopian Artificial Intelligence Institute)
items.abstract: This work presents high-quality Text to Speech (TTS) systems for Amharic and Afan Oromo, two widely spoken but under-resourced languages in Ethiopia using the SpeechT5, a Transformer-based self-supervised model. A phonetically rich and diverse text corpus was created, then professionally recorded in a studio to produce 200 hours of high-quality speech data (100 per language). To resolve linguistic complexities such as gemination and context-sensitive pronunciation in Amharic,we created a special dataset and extended the training to 113 hours. We evaluated the models both objectively and subjectively. Human raters assigned mean opinion scores of 4.65 for Amharic and 4.43 for Afan Oromo, highlighting the naturalness, intelligibility, and accurate pronunciation of the models. These results demonstrate that linguistically informed data combined with self-supervised learning enables robust, natural-sounding TTS for low-resource languages.

items.title: IN-F5: Adapting an English TTS Foundation Model for Multilingual and Zero-Resource Indian Speech Synthesis
items.authors: Praveen Srinivasa Varadhan(AI4Bharat, WSAI, Indian Institute of Technology Madras); Srija Anand(AI4Bharat, WSAI, Indian Institute of Technology Madras); Siddhartha Soma(Saryps Labs); Mitesh M Khapra(AI4Bharat, WSAI, Indian Institute of Technology Madras)
items.abstract: We investigate whether an English TTS foundation model (F5-TTS) can serve as an effective prior for low-resource multilingual speech synthesis. Starting from an English-pretrained checkpoint, we adapt to 11 Indian languages using less than 2% of the original pretraining data scale. Through a controlled comparison of training from scratch, direct fine-tuning, and fine-tuning with continued English exposure, we find that direct fine-tuning on Indian data alone performs best, challenging the assumption that multilingual systems benefit from continued high-resource exposure. Extensive subjective and objective evaluations show that the resulting model, IN-F5, approaches human-level naturalness and speaker similarity while exhibiting emergent capabilities including polyglot voice transfer, code-mixing, and expressive style control. We analyze data scaling and demonstrate zero-resource cross-lingual transfer to Bhojpuri and Tulu to extend TTS to under-represented languages.

title: Speech Synthesis Evaluation 1
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 7 - Oral 5 - Speech Synthesis Evaluation 1

items.title: Preferences of a Voice-First Nation: Large-Scale Pairwise Evaluation and Preference Analysis for TTS in Indian Languages
items.authors: Srija Anand(IIT Madras; AI4Bharat); Ashwin Sankar(IIT Madras; AI4Bharat); Ishvinder Sethi(AI4Bharat); Aaditya Pareek(Josh Talks); Kartik Rajput(AI4Bharat); Gaurav Yadav(Josh Talks); Nikhil Narasimhan(AI4Bharat); Adish Pandya(IIT Madras); Deepon Halder(IIT Madras); Mohammed Safi Ur Rahman Khan(IIT Madras; AI4Bharat); Praveen S V(IIT Madras; AI4Bharat); Shobhit Banga(Josh Talks); Mitesh M Khapra(IIT Madras; AI4Bharat)
items.abstract: Crowdsourced pairwise evaluation has emerged as a scalable approach for assessing foundation models. However, applying it to Text to Speech(TTS) introduces high variance due to linguistic diversity and multidimensional nature of speech perception. We present a controlled multidimensional pairwise evaluation framework for multilingual TTS that combines linguistic control with perceptually grounded annotation. Using 5K+ native and code-mixed sentences across 10 Indic languages, we evaluate 7 state-of-the-art TTS systems and collect over 120K pairwise comparisons from over 1900 native raters. In addition to overall preference, raters provide judgments across 6 perceptual dimensions: intelligibility, expressiveness, voice quality, liveliness, noise, and hallucinations. Using Bradley-Terry modeling, we construct a multilingual leaderboard, interpret human preference using SHAP analysis and analyze leaderboard reliability alongside model strengths and trade-offs across perceptual dimensions.

items.title: Application context in speech synthesis evaluation: A problem and a solution
items.authors: Fritz Seebauer(Bielefeld University); Markus Rothgänger(Bielefeld University); Sven Wachsmuth(Bielefeld University); Petra Wagner(Bielefeld University)
items.abstract: Advancements in research of synthetic speech can only be properly quantified and driven by well-proven evaluation procedures, the most prevalent of which being the subjective listening test. In this paper, the ecological validity of such tests is evaluated empirically in an experiment comparing rating outcomes of four synthetic speech systems across four different application contexts. It is shown that, depending on the scenario in which they are obtained, the ratings for a respective synthesis system change significantly. Additionally, it is found that the impact of the application also depends on the system in question, highlighting a potential confound in evaluations comparing systems without a specified application context. Further, it is discovered that ratings collected in a digital twin provide statistically equivalent ratings to the ones obtained in a physical setting, suggesting that simulation testing might prove a beneficial path to achieving ecologically valid evaluations.

items.title: Is Natural Always Appropriate? Investigating Naturalness and Appropriateness Across Different Domains for TTS Evaluation
items.authors: Dominika Woszczyk(Iconic); Andreas Triantafyllopoulos(TUM); Jura Miniota(KTH); Éva Székely(KTH); Bjoern Schuller(TUM; Imperial College London)
items.abstract: Text-to-speech (TTS) evaluation is an open challenge. While the primary target was "naturalness," recent fidelity gains shifted focus toward "appropriateness" and whether speech is correct for its context. In this work, we examine how perception changes when the expected downstream use varies. We measure the appropriateness and human-likeness of five SOTA TTS systems across five domains: AI assistant, reader, actor, animated character, and spontaneous speaker. Results show appropriateness varies across domains independently of naturalness. While systems shine at reading, expressive domains remain challenging, and optimizing for one can degrade others. Furthermore, naturalness scores tend to penalize stylized speech while rewarding spontaneity. Finally, our study also highlights blind spots in one-size-fits-all evaluation metrics across more expressive domains. We demonstrate that TTS performance is not "solved" but depends on the target domain, requiring context-aware evaluation.

items.title: NV-Bench: Benchmark of Nonverbal Vocalization Synthesis for Expressive Text-to-Speech Generation
items.authors: Qinke Ni(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen); Huan Liao(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen); Dekun Chen(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen); Yuxiang Wang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen); Zhizheng Wu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen; Shenzhen Loop Area Institute; Amphion Technology Co.,Ltd)
items.abstract: While recent text-to-speech (TTS) systems increasingly integrate nonverbal vocalizations (NVs), their evaluations lack standardized metrics and reliable ground-truth references. To bridge this gap, we propose NV-Bench, the first benchmark grounded in a functional taxonomy that treats NVs as communicative acts rather than acoustic artifacts. NV-Bench comprises 1,651 multi-lingual, in-the-wild utterances with paired human reference audio, balanced across 14 NV categories. We introduce a dual-dimensional evaluation protocol: (1) Instruction Alignment, utilizing the proposed paralinguistic character error rate (PCER) to assess controllability, (2) Acoustic Fidelity, measuring the distributional gap to real recordings to assess acoustic realism. We evaluate diverse TTS models and develop two baselines. Experimental results demonstrate a strong correlation between our objective metrics and human perception, establishing NV-Bench as a standardized evaluation framework.

items.title: Phonetically Grounded Vowel Space Metrics for Evaluating Synthetic Speech During TTS Model Training
items.authors: Pasindu Udawatta(University of Auckland); Jesin James(University of Auckland); Ake Nicholas(University of Auckland); B. T. Balamurali(Independent Researcher); C. I. Watson(University of Auckland)
items.abstract: Synthetic speech is generally evaluated using subjective listening tests, which are costly and impractical to perform during text-to-speech (TTS) model training. Traditional loss curves in model training lack linguistic interpretability and fail to reflect perceptual changes. We propose using phonetically grounded objective metrics, Vowel Space Overlap and Procrustes Normalised Disparity, to evaluate synthetic speech during training by quantifying the similarity between synthesised and ground-truth vowel space shapes. We fine-tuned a TTS model on two accents, computed the metrics at training steps, and conducted perception tests to assess the relationship between the metrics and perceived accent similarity. Our results show significant correlations between metrics and accent perception across both accents. This suggests that the proposed metrics provide reliable, perceptually meaningful, and interpretable complements to loss curves for evaluating synthetic speech during training.

items.title: The Binding Effect: Analysis of How Multi-Dimensional Cues Form Gender Bias in Instruction TTS
items.authors: Kuan-Yu Chen(National Taiwan University; Inventec Corporation); Yi-Cheng Lin(National Taiwan University); Po-Chung Hsieh(National Taiwan University); Huang-Cheng Chou(University of Southern California); Chih-Fan Hsu(Inventec Corporation); Jeng-Lin Li(Inventec Corporation); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University); Jian-Jiun Ding(National Taiwan University)
items.abstract: Current bias evaluations in Instruction Text-to-Speech (ITTS) often rely on univariate testing, overlooking the compositional structure of social cues. In this work, we investigate gender bias by modeling prompts as combinations of Social Status, Career stereotypes, and Persona descriptors. Analyzing open-source ITTS models, we uncover systematic interaction effects where social dimensions modulate one another, creating complex bias patterns missed by univariate baselines. Crucially, our findings indicate that these biases extend beyond surface-level artifacts, demonstrating strong associations with the semantic priors of pre-trained text encoders and the skewed distributions inherent in training data. We further demonstrate that generic diversity prompting is insufficient to override these entrenched patterns, underscoring the need for compositional analysis to diagnose latent risks in generative speech.

title: Audio Language Models
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 8 - Oral 1 - Audio Language Models

items.title: Recent advances in speech language model for ASR
items.abstract: With recent advances in large language models (LLMs), both academia and industry have increasingly focused on developing speech LLMs by integrating the speech modality into LLM architectures. This talk centers on recent progress in speech-LLM for automatic speech recognition (ASR). While standard speech-LLM approaches have reached maturity, as evidenced by state-of-the-art results on major leaderboards, I will delve into topics such as unleashing the full potential of LLMs, long-form speech modeling, and decoding acceleration. I will also introduce recent breakthroughs in encoder-free speech-LLMs, which pave the way toward truly native multimodal language models that process speech as naturally as text.

items.title: HybridCodec: Modeling Discrete and Continuous Representations For Efficient Speech Language Models
items.authors: Artem Ploujnikov(Mila Quebec AI Institute; Concordia University); Francesco Verdini(Sapienza University of Rome); Samir Sadok(Inria, Université Grenoble Alpes CNRS); Mirco Ravanelli(Mila Quebec AI Institute; Concordia University)
items.abstract: Discrete audio representations have become increasingly popular for building multimodal text-audio systems and integrating audio capabilities into Large Language Models (LLMs). However, numerous studies report performance degradation on various downstream tasks due to information loss during discretization. To address this, we propose a novel approach combining temporally compressed discrete tokens with dimensionality-reduced continuous residuals. Our framework consists of a hybridized discrete-continuous focal modulation codec and a hybrid Transformer. This architecture performs autoregressive inference in the discrete domain, coupled with non-autoregressive prediction and continuous residual upsampling. Experimental results show that our approach significantly improves the retention of speaker characteristics compared to discrete-only methods, while simultaneously reducing the number of required autoregressive steps.

items.title: TASTE-Streaming: Towards Streamable Text-Aligned Speech Tokenization and Embedding for Spoken Language Modeling
items.authors: Liang-Hsuan Tseng(National Taiwan University); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University)
items.abstract: Text-speech joint spoken language modeling (SLM) aims at natural and intelligent speech-based interactions, but developing such a system may suffer from modality mismatch: speech unit sequences are much longer than text tokens. Prior work reduces this gap with text-aligned tokenization and embedding (TASTE), producing speech tokens that align in lengths with their textual counterparts. However, the dependence on an external ASR system and the use of a non-causal decoder limits streaming use. To address this limitation, we propose TASTE-S, a streamable extension of TASTE suitable for real-time usage. TASTE-S integrates a CTC-based ASR module into the encoder for instant dual-modality encoding. We also redesign the unit decoder to enable on-the-fly decoding. With joint training, we show that TASTE-S matches TASTE's performance while significantly reducing latency. Further investigations reveal that TASTE-S remains robust to transcriptions and enables long-form encoding and decoding.

items.title: Investigating Faithfulness in Large Audio Language Models
items.authors: Pooneh Mousavi(Concordia University; Mila - Quebec AI Institute); Lovenya Jain(Birla Institute of Technology and Science); Mirco Ravanelli(Concordia University; Mila - Quebec AI Institute); Cem Subakan(Université Laval; Mila - Quebec AI Institute)
items.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) integrate audio encoders with pretrained Large Language Models to perform complex multimodal reasoning tasks. While these models can generate Chain-of-Thought (CoT) explanations, the faithfulness of these reasoning chains remains unclear. In this work, we propose a systematic framework to evaluate CoT faithfulness in LALMs with respect to both the input audio and the final model prediction. We define three criteria for audio faithfulness: hallucination-free, holistic, and attentive listening. We also introduce a benchmark based on both audio and CoT interventions to assess faithfulness¹. Experiments on Audio Flamingo 3 and Qwen2.5-Omni suggest a potential multimodal disconnect: reasoning often aligns with the final prediction but is not always strongly grounded in the audio and can be vulnerable to hallucinations or adversarial perturbations.

items.title: IndicContextEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating Context Utilisation in Audio Large Language Models Across 8 Indic Languages
items.authors: Sakshi Joshi(IIT Madras); Dhruv Subhash Rathi(Sarvam AI); Sanskar Singh(Sarvam AI); Eldho Ittan George(AI4Bharat); R J Hari(IIT Madras); Kaushal Bhogale(IIT Madras); Mitesh M. Khapra(IIT Madras)
items.abstract: AudioLLMs enable speech recognition conditioned on textual prompts such as domain descriptions or entity lists. However, it remains unclear whether these models genuinely utilise such context or rely on parametric knowledge learned during pretraining. Existing benchmarks cannot answer this question because they evaluate transcription under fixed prompting conditions and rarely include explicit contextual inputs. We introduce IndicContextEval, a 56-hour multilingual benchmark of natural speech from 555 speakers across 8 Indian languages and 23 professional domains. We design a 7-level prompting framework that progressively introduces contextual signals, including metadata, natural-language descriptions, entity lists in English and native script, and adversarial prompts with incorrect entities. Evaluating five models reveals substantial differences in context utilisation behaviour, highlighting the need for explicit evaluation of contextual grounding in AudioLLMs.

title: Clinically Useful Speech Representations 2
header: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 13 - Oral 8 - Clinically Useful Speech Representations 2

items.title: Clinically meaningful speech representations
items.abstract: While modern speech models can learn powerful representations that achieve impressive predictive performance, high accuracy alone has not translated into widespread clinical adoption. Bridging this gap requires representations that are interpretable, robust across populations, tasks, languages, and recording conditions, sensitive to clinically meaningful change, reliable across participants longitudinally, validated against relevant clinical constructs and outcomes, and ultimately, used to support decisions in real-world studies. This talk surveys the evolution of clinically meaningful speech representations, illustrating key developments with examples from research across ALS, Parkinson’s disease, schizophrenia, depression, autism, and cognitive impairment. We will examine approaches and challenges to combining the power of state-of-the-art models, composite measures and scalable multimodal assessment on the one hand with interpretability, psychometric rigor, and clinical validation on the other in order to transform speech representations from merely being compelling lab research into becoming useful real-world clinical tools.

items.title: Reducing Measurement Noise in Digital Speech Biomarkers: Interpretable Composite Index Scores for Longitudinal ALS Monitoring in Clinical Trials
items.authors: Michael Neumann(Modality.AI); Hardik Kothare(Modality.AI); Diego Cadavid(Verge Genomics); Robert H. Scannevin(Verge Genomics); Anil Tarachandani(Verge Genomics); Ines Hoffmann(Verge Genomics); Tara Haley(Verge Genomics); Shane Raines(2b Analytics); Vikram Ramanarayanan(Modality.AI; University of California)
items.abstract: Digital speech measures are promising for remote monitoring of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, single speech features can be sensitive to measurement noise. In this work, composite index scores, with feature weights estimated from a natural history dataset, were evaluated for reliability, measurement error, and their ability to capture disease progression on the VRG50635 ALS clinical trial data. We conducted a systematic psychometric evaluation to quantify measurement error reduction in composite scores relative to their constituent features. Linear mixed effects models were applied to assess longitudinal change relative to the ALSFRS-R. The results show that index scores have excellent ICC (> 0.9) and reduce the MDC compared to individual features, while maintaining sensitivity to track longitudinal changes. Our findings show that composite index scores can be applied across datasets and provide great potential as robust endpoints in clinical trials.

items.title: Task-Conditioned Audio-Text-Image Fusion for Cognitive Score Estimation from Speech-Based Assessments
items.authors: Justyna Krzywdziak(AGH University of Krakow; Samsung R&D Institute); Władysław Średniawa(Samsung R&D Institute); Agnieszka Pruszek(Samsung R&D Institute); Wojciech Szecówka(AGH University of Krakow; Samsung R&D Institute); Michał Grzeszczyk(Samsung R&D Institute); Teresa Brzozka(Samsung R&D Institute); Bartłomiej Eljasiak(Samsung R&D Institute); Zofia Marciniak(Samsung R&D Institute); Łukasz Lazarski(Samsung R&D Institute); Mateusz Matuszewski(Samsung R&D Institute); Daria Hemmerling(AGH University of Krakow; Samsung R&D Institute)
items.abstract: People with mild cognitive impariment tend to perform speech-based tasks differently than the healthy population. In picture description tasks, they often describe a narrower portion of the scene, missing details and spatial relations. We propose a multimodal framework for estimating cognitive assessment scores (MoCA and MMSE) from speech-based cognitive tasks. The model uses pretrained encoders for audio, text, and optional vision, followed by modality-specific projections and task-conditioned fusion. We compare staged variants from acoustic features to foundation-model embeddings, late fusion, mid-level cross-attention fusion, and a final mixture-of-experts model. We also introduce a label-conditioned image-text alignment loss for picture description samples to model differences in transcript-image consistency between healthy controls and patients with mild cognitive impairment. The best model achieved 2.11(+-0.03) MoCA RMSE and 1.85(+-0.08) MMSE RMSE in picture description task.

items.title: Analyzing Longitudinal Vocal Changes During Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Hikikomori Patients
items.authors: Samara S. Leal(University of Milan); Stavros Ntalampiras(University of Milan); Antonio Trabacca(Scientific Institute IRCCS “E. Medea”, Scientific Direction); Marcella Bellani(University of Verona; AOUI); Roberto Sassi(University of Milan)
items.abstract: Monitoring treatment response during Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is challenging due to the lack of objective, temporally grounded markers. This study investigates longitudinal vocal dynamics in hikikomori patients undergoing CBT using session-level speech recordings. First, stable Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs) that exhibited consistent temporal variation and low early inter-subject variability were identified. Trajectory analyses then revealed distinct speech evolution patterns between patients showing clinical improvement or deterioration. Finally, Wav2vec 2.0 embeddings were compared with traditional acoustic features. The fusion of Wav2vec 2.0 with MFCCs and fundamental frequency (F0) achieved the highest F1-score across age and gender groups, indicating the complementary value of deep and hand-crafted descriptors. Overall, treatment outcomes were captured more accurately by trajectory evolution than by static pre-post differences.

items.title: Acoustic Biomarkers of Sleep Deprivation on French Read Speech: Interpretable and Frugal Modeling of Sleep Deprivation and Its Symptoms
items.authors: Vincent P. Martin(INRIA Nancy, LORIA; UMons); Jean-Luc Rouas(LaBRI; CNRS); Pierre Philip(SANPSY; CHU de Bordeaux)
items.abstract: Sleep deprivation and its consequences are a major public and personal health issue. In this study, we draw on the SOMVOICE corpus to estimate sleep deprivation and its symptoms (sleepiness, fatigue, performance loss) using speech samples. We prioritised interpretability and frugality, using simple yet robust and validated acoustic features (eGeMAPS and Snack) and classifiers (SVM, Random Forest, Gradient Boost). We evaluated the sex-and age-related biases of our classifier, and reported our energy consumption and carbon footprint. Using SHAP values, we investigated the relative importance of each feature to the classification, allowing comparison with previous studies and driving the field towards mechanistic approaches. Finally, using a symptom network and performing cross-task evaluation, we investigated whether the classifiers had generalised the task they had been trained on, or a more general, less specific construct.
